title: Mandhana Says India Have 'A Lot to Learn.' Edulji Says It Starts With the Openers. The T20 World Cup Begins in Six Days.
excerpt: India lost the T20I series to England 2-1 but leave with match practice, a clear understanding of conditions, and an opener against Pakistan in Birmingham that is already sold out.
body:
India's preparation for the ICC Women's T20 World Cup landed somewhere between productive and sobering. The 2-1 T20I series loss to England exposed familiar vulnerabilities but also handed the squad exactly what it came looking for — competitive cricket in the conditions where the tournament begins on June 12.

## The Openers Are the Problem Everyone Sees

Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma managed a combined 75 runs across the three-match series. Neither converted a start. For a team built around the firepower of its top order, that number was difficult to ignore.

Mandhana did not try to hide it. "We both are timing the ball well but unfortunately are not able to contribute in big ways for the team," she said after the third T20I in Taunton. "For both of us, we'll go back in the nets and keep working hard and make sure that we come back better as an opening pair."

Former India captain Diana Edulji, speaking on the sidelines of a BBC Research report on Indian women in sport, was more direct. "Smriti and Shafali need to get quickly into form, and once they start getting into form, I think that will help India win at the T20 World Cup," she said. For Edulji, the equation is straightforward: India's batting begins and ends with its openers. If they fire, the middle order has a platform. If they don't, the pressure shifts to everyone else.

## The Middle Order Gave More Than It Got Credit For

While the opening pair struggled, the rest of India's batting showed encouraging signs. Jemimah Rodrigues continued an impressive run of form that stretches back to the 2025 ODI World Cup final, where her 87 earned her Player of the Match. She has batted at three, four, and five across recent series and insists she is comfortable with all of them. "I think I'm comfortable at all positions," she said. "Now is the time where we have a few more games to experiment about what's the best combination."

Yastika Bhatia's return to international cricket after a long injury layoff was another positive. Rodrigues described her presence as a "great advantage" and praised the character it took to perform immediately after such an absence.

Captain Harmanpreet Kaur delivered a reminder of her best in the deciding match. Walking in after early wickets left India under pressure, she anchored the innings with an unbeaten 56 that guided the visitors to 180. Mandhana acknowledged the significance: "Harman when she's at her best, it's a sight to watch. Really important innings under pressure."

## The Bowling Needs a Drawing Board

India reduced England to 38 for 3 during the third-match chase. A match-winning 137-run partnership between Heather Knight and Alice Capsey turned the contest decisively. England reached the target with six wickets in hand and nine balls to spare. The collapse was clinical and instructive.

Mandhana admitted the bowling group would revisit its plans. "On bowling, we'll go to the drawing board and see which options are better. We did that before this series, maybe we can go back again. Now I think I know in these conditions what balls are to be bowled."

Nandni Sharma, the uncapped 24-year-old pacer from Chandigarh who took 17 wickets in WPL 2026 for Delhi Capitals, is the wildcard in India's bowling attack. If conditions in England offer seam and swing, her inclusion could prove decisive.

## Group of Death or Group of Opportunity

India are in Group 1 alongside six-time champions Australia, South Africa, Bangladesh, the Netherlands, and Pakistan. On paper, it is the tougher half of the draw. Edulji waved away the concern. "All the teams are going to be strong. T20 is a format where the weakest team can beat the strongest team on that day," she said.

India's opener against Pakistan on June 14 at Edgbaston in Birmingham is already sold out. Mandhana looked forward to the occasion. "We did play Pakistan in Birmingham, and it was a sell-out. Not just India-Pakistan, we really need to hype up the T20 World Cup. I'm sure a lot of people will come and watch us play."

## What NRIs in the UK Should Know

The tournament runs from June 12 to July 5 across venues in England. For the Indian diaspora in the UK, it is a rare chance to watch the reigning ODI World Cup champions play a global tournament in their backyard. India's group-stage matches are scheduled at Edgbaston (Birmingham) and other English venues, with fixtures against Pakistan, Australia, South Africa, Bangladesh, and the Netherlands.

Tickets for India's matches have been in high demand. The India-Pakistan clash in particular is expected to be one of the tournament's marquee events, with diaspora communities across Birmingham, London, and Leicester driving ticket sales.

India won their maiden Women's ODI World Cup in 2025. The T20 crown would complete a rare double. But as Mandhana put it: "We have a lot to learn."
